steps.explanationAfterStep: Nitrogen now has four bonds and no lone pair, so it carries the positive charge. This is an ammonium salt, not yet an amine.
Methylamine is free. It is itself a nucleophile, often a better one than ammonia, so it can react with more iodomethane: a large excess of ammonia keeps this over-alkylation down.

title: Ammonia and iodomethane
subtitle: SN2, then a proton transfer frees the amine
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15

reactants.caption: ammonia (two molecules) + iodomethane
hintTiers: Which atom of ammonia has a lone pair, and which carbon is δ+?
Nitrogen attacks the carbon as the C–I bond breaks: an SN2 step. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: the nitrogen lone pair forms a bond to the carbon. Arrow 2: the C–I bond breaks, and its pair goes onto iodine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Ammonia attacks iodomethane. Draw the first step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Iodine is the leaving group. Nitrogen attacks the δ+ carbon bonded to it.
The C–I pair leaves with iodine, which can hold the negative charge.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Octet check: carbon would now have 10 electrons. What has to leave as the nucleophile arrives?

ammonium-salt.caption: methylammonium iodide + ammonia
hintTiers: A positively charged N–H is acidic. Which species present is a base?
The second ammonia takes the proton from the positive nitrogen; the N–H pair stays on that nitrogen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: the lone pair of the free ammonia forms a bond to the hydrogen on the positive nitrogen. Arrow 2: that N–H bond breaks, and its pair goes back onto the nitrogen.
ammonium-salt.learnerPrompt: The nitrogen still carries an extra proton. Remove it.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Iodide is the conjugate base of HI, a very strong acid, so it is far too weak a base. Ammonia, used in excess, takes the proton.
The carbon now has four bonds and no leaving group. Here the second ammonia acts as a base, on the N–H hydrogen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right base, right proton. Hydrogen can only have one bond: where does the old N–H pair go?

mechanismSummary: Alkylation of ammonia: SN2 gives an ammonium salt, then a proton transfer to a second ammonia frees the amine. The product amine is still nucleophilic, so mixtures of more highly alkylated amines form unless ammonia is used in large excess.
